A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same SCRIPTS benchmark and model-evaluation study. Their main text, figures, tables, and Appendices A–D are readable and support reliable matching across revisions and relocations.

before.justification: V1 reports original model evaluations, annotation-agreement measurements, failure analyses, and social-information experiments, including Appendix Tables 10–15.

after.justification: V3 retains these original experiments and adds model evaluations, CoT results, and relationship-label agreement measurements in Tables 6–8.

M1.justification: The three-tier annotation scheme, label aggregation, open-ended inference, GPT-4o judging, and social-information prompting remain substantively unchanged. V3's 27-item annotation inventory matches the list already present in v1 Table 9; the revised description does not establish a redesigned method.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same 60 movies and 1,147 dialogues: 580 English and 567 Korean, including three-speaker scenes with dyadic relationship inference. The appendix movie inventories match. Additional models and the original Korean text of an existing example do not expand dataset or task coverage.

E2.justification: V3 Table 7 adds GPT-4.1, GPT-5, Qwen3-32B, Llama3.3-70B-Instruct, and Kanana2-30B-A3B-Instruct to the comparison in v1 Table 10. The latter three also enter the CoT comparison in v3 Table 8, substantially expanding the evaluated comparator set.

E3.justification: New comparisons include larger configurations such as Qwen3-32B and Llama3.3-70B. V3 also revises the stated annotation inventory from 50 to 27, matching v1's appendix, and describes the agreement-table subset as two annotators selecting non-neutral labels rather than two agreeing. These reported setting revisions do not establish reruns of retained experiments.

E4.justification: V3 extends the CoT ablation to three additional models and adds agreement analysis for the relationship labels themselves. The four failure modes, 30-case error analysis, social-information interventions, and logistic regressions are retained. Moving the diversity and regression analyses into appendices does not constitute new analysis.

E5.justification: V3 adds mean pairwise Jaccard agreement for HIGHLY LIKELY and UNLIKELY label sets and bootstrap significance reporting for thinking comparisons (p > 0.05). Appendix B.3 also changes the stated referent of 96% agreement from agreement between authors to judge–human agreement. The five-response main evaluation and single-run thinking design remain unchanged.

E6.justification: Tables 7–8 add substantial benchmark and CoT results: GPT-4.1, for example, has newly reported HIGHLY LIKELY rates of 0.819 English and 0.783 Korean. Table 6 adds relationship-label Jaccard scores. Shared model-result rows remain equivalent apart from rounding, while the introduction corrects Llama's English figure from 45% to 41.3%, consistent with v1 Table 10.

T1.justification: Neither version presents formal theorems, proofs, or substantive mathematical derivations. The added Jaccard and bootstrap reporting concerns empirical statistical analysis, without introducing new formal theory.

C1.justification: The principal benchmark contribution and findings about social-reasoning failures remain. V3 removes the conclusion's explicit claim that Korean-specialized models improve on Korean relative to their English performance. Its abstract also drops 'proprietary' from the models associated with the 75–80% English and 58–69% Korean accuracy ranges, changing that claim's stated scope.

C2.justification: V3 adds the limitation that movie scripts may not represent real conversations, explains their practicality as a proxy, and proposes more specific inference- and training-time improvements. It also qualifies thinking differences as statistically non-significant. The CoT-faithfulness caveat already appeared in a v1 footnote and is relocated to Limitations.

D1.justification: V3 adds a direct Hugging Face dataset link, recruitment-announcement and payment-platform information, exact compensation rates, and the original Korean dialogue supporting an existing case study. Label-normalization documentation is expanded. The main-text inference prompt and five-label annotation allowance were already documented in v1's appendix.

R1.justification: V3 substantially contracts the research positioning: it removes the Theory-of-Mind discussion, the subsection connecting varying-plausibility evaluation to translation and dialogue evaluation, and v1's dataset-comparison Table 1. Associated works including Jung et al., Kim et al., Freitag et al., and Zhang et al. disappear. Core social-relationship benchmark comparisons remain, and a group-chat application citation is added.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, related work, annotation description, and conclusion undergo extensive rewriting. Diversity material and regression discussion move from the main text into appendices, the annotation appendix is reorganized, and acknowledgements are added. These constitute substantial editorial restructuring despite retention of the central study.

P2.justification: V3 removes the dataset-comparison table, converts v1 Table 5 into Figure 4's point plot, relocates the diversity chart and regression table, and restructures the agreement and model-result tables. It also redraws the error chart and adds prominent prompt and recruitment boxes. These are substantial display changes; relocated and replotted results are largely retained.

improvement.justification: V3 improves transparency and empirical support through relationship-label agreement reporting, broader model comparisons, clearer annotation and access information, and a substantive movie-script limitation. The gains are tempered by reduced related-work context, limited configuration and bootstrap details for new material, and the abstract's loss of the 'proprietary' qualification. Overall, the evidence supports a modest net improvement.
